metadata.name: Building Scalable Microservices with Kotlin and Ktor

attributes.description: A comprehensive guide to designing and building production-ready microservices using Kotlin and the Ktor framework, covering service discovery, resilience patterns, and deployment strategies.

document.title: Building Scalable Microservices with Kotlin and Ktor

content.text: Building Scalable Microservices with Kotlin and Ktor

Microservices architecture has become the de facto standard for building large-scale distributed systems. In this article, we explore how Kotlin and the Ktor framework provide an excellent foundation for building lightweight, performant microservices that can scale to meet the demands of modern applications.
Why Kotlin for Microservices?

Kotlin's coroutine-based concurrency model is a natural fit for microservices. Unlike traditional thread-per-request models, coroutines allow you to handle thousands of concurrent connections with minimal memory overhead. Combined with Ktor's lightweight, non-blocking architecture, you get a framework that starts in milliseconds and uses a fraction of the resources compared to traditional servlet-based frameworks.
Service Discovery and Communication

In a microservices architecture, services need to discover and communicate with each other dynamically. We'll look at how to integrate with service discovery mechanisms like Consul or Kubernetes DNS, and how to implement resilient inter-service communication using circuit breakers and retry policies.
Resilience Patterns

Production microservices must handle failures gracefully. We cover essential resilience patterns including circuit breakers to prevent cascade failures, bulkhead isolation to limit blast radius, timeout policies to avoid hanging requests, and retry strategies with exponential backoff for transient failures.
Deployment and Observability

We conclude with deployment strategies including containerization with Docker, orchestration with Kubernetes, and implementing observability through structured logging, distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, and metrics collection with Prometheus. These practices ensure your microservices are not just running, but running well.

metadata.name: Building an Accessible Design System from Scratch

attributes.description: Learn how to create a design system that prioritizes accessibility from day one, with practical examples of color systems, component APIs, and testing strategies.

document.title: Building an Accessible Design System from Scratch

content.text: Building an Accessible Design System from Scratch

Design systems are the backbone of consistent, scalable user interfaces. But too often, accessibility is treated as an afterthought — bolted on after components are built rather than woven into the foundation. In this guide, we take a different approach: building accessibility into every layer of a design system from the very beginning.
The Accessible Color System

Color is one of the most fundamental elements of any design system, and getting it right for accessibility means more than just checking contrast ratios. We build a color palette system that automatically ensures WCAG AA compliance, provides semantic color tokens that work across light and dark themes, and includes utilities for checking contrast programmatically.
Component API Design

The way we design component APIs has a profound impact on accessibility outcomes. By making accessible patterns the default and requiring explicit opt-out for less accessible alternatives, we create a system where doing the right thing is easier than doing the wrong thing. We explore patterns for focus management, keyboard navigation, and screen reader announcements.
Testing for Accessibility

Automated testing catches many accessibility issues, but not all. We set up a comprehensive testing strategy combining automated axe-core scans in CI, visual regression testing for color contrast, keyboard navigation integration tests, and manual testing protocols with screen readers. This multi-layered approach ensures that accessibility regressions are caught early and often.

metadata.name: Getting Started with GraphQL: A Practical Tutorial

attributes.description: A hands-on tutorial for building your first GraphQL API, covering schema design, resolvers, queries, mutations, and client-side data fetching.

document.title: Getting Started with GraphQL: A Practical Tutorial

content.text: Getting Started with GraphQL: A Practical Tutorial

GraphQL has transformed how we think about API design. Instead of juggling multiple REST endpoints, clients can request exactly the data they need in a single query. In this tutorial, we build a complete GraphQL API from scratch, covering everything from schema design to client integration.
Designing Your Schema

The schema is the contract between your API and its clients. We start by defining types that model our domain — a blog with posts, authors, and comments. We'll explore best practices for naming conventions, nullability decisions, and when to use interfaces versus unions.
Writing Resolvers

Resolvers are the functions that fetch data for each field in your schema. We implement resolvers for our blog types, demonstrating how to handle relationships efficiently using data loaders to avoid the N+1 query problem. We also cover error handling patterns and how to return meaningful error messages to clients.
Queries and Mutations

With our schema and resolvers in place, we implement query operations for fetching posts with filtering and pagination, and mutation operations for creating and updating content. We demonstrate input validation, optimistic updates, and how to structure mutation responses for the best client experience.
Client-Side Integration

Finally, we connect our API to a client application using Apollo Client. We cover query and mutation hooks, cache management, optimistic UI updates, and real-time subscriptions. By the end, you'll have a fully functional GraphQL stack running end to end.
